doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: African drumming as language and the roots of jazz
summary: Harper tells students to study jazz history starting in Africa, mentions Alioune Faye's family, and says jazz should say something.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah, they just had a fellow at Hamilton last week with an mbira and he basically was saying the same thing, that the scale intonation can actually vary from one village to the next.

Yeah. Which is really, really nice and slick in itself. Because everything has an identity. And I guess for a lot of them, they hear them and they can tell, okay I know that sound, I know where that’s coming from. But it’s the same way with the music, which is interesting too. Because even with the drummers, that’s why with a lot of my students I tell them they have to go — because I got it from Jackie — they have to go study the history of this music. If you really want to play this music and play it well and with the best intentions, you have to do a study of jazz history. And you can’t do that without starting in Africa. Because for them, when they play those drums, it’s a language. They’re talking. Those guys will sit down and they’re playing stuff and people that know them will hear them and they’ll know what they’re saying. You know what I mean? So it’s very, very interesting. Because as you know from checking out some of my CD’s, I have used a lot of different African drummers over the years. And one of the last guys I used, Alioune Faye, his whole family plays. And there have been times when we would get to different cities where some of his family is living and they’ll come and sit in. You know we’ll do workshops and I’ll let them play. And they’ll break it down, they’ll tell us, well if he plays this I know he’s calling me. That’s my name. So it’s really slick and interesting.

My daughter actually plays in an African drum ensemble in Rochester. And I go to see them. It’s led by a fellow from West Africa. And it would annoy me — the music was incredible but I would get annoyed when I couldn’t put — where’s 1? You know, I’d lose it. And I don’t think I should be annoyed but I kept trying to codify it into something I could feel like I understood.

Yeah, for them it’s there. It’s just like, you know, they have whatever that clave is, that gets held down, because one of those instruments usually is holding everything down, where you can say okay — but then all of them polyrhythms go on top. And that’s where you start to hear all these other voices. But there’s something nailing it, holding it down. But it’s so interesting. And that’s what jazz, how jazz evolved, out of that. Jazz is still a language. It’s speaking. It should be saying something. And sometimes my problem with some of the stuff that comes out today, sometimes I don’t think people think about that and they’re not really trying to say anything. When you go back and you listen to Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker, John Coltrane, you know, and guys we talked about, Harry “Sweets” Edison and Frank Wess. They were saying something. There was some intent. It wasn’t just I’m just going to get up here and have a good time. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
You know it was that, it was a part of that, but there was still some other very meaningful —
